I beg leave to introduce Bill No. 76 to amend the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Explain.

The Bill relates
to the publication of defamatory libels in judicial proceedings. Its purpose is to amend section 320 of the Criminal Code. That section reads as follows:
No one commits an offence by publishing any defamatory matter, in any proceeding held before or under the authority of any court exercising judicial authority, or in any inquiry made under the authority of any statute or by order of His Majesty, or of any of the Departments of Government, Dominion or provincial.
My intention to add the following words after this section.
Provided he also publishes at the same time any facts, extenuating circumstances or argument, which the person likely to he injured by such defamatory matter is entitled to set up before such court or at such enquiry.
As the law now reads great damage and injury may be done without possible redress. An individual can lay a complaint before the court and adduce his evidence, and the accused may find it necessary to ask for an adjournment, in which case the evidence goes to the public without his defence being published. I might say that

an hon. member only a few days ago was greatly injured by such publication. The purpose of the Bill is to prevent the publication of such damaging evidence unaccompanied by the defence or facts that the accused may be entitled to set up.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. H. S. BELAND (Beauce) moved for leave to introduce a Bill to amend the Maple Products Act, 1920.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the law as it stands to-day permits the use of the word "maple" only in reference to those articles of food which are composed wholly of pure maple sugar or maple syrup. The present Bill is not a restrictive measure, it is rather designed to facilitate the sale and purchase of maple products, but as the present law precludes the use of the word "maple" in conjunction with other words, the House will readily see that an article of food containing a proportion of maple sugar or maple syrup cannot be so designated. The experience of the working of this measure during the past year has been that the new law constitutes a hindrance to the easy marketing of the pure article. If I read to the House the main paragraph of the proposed amendment its purpose will be readily appreciated. It is in this form:
The word "maple" may be used in combination with other word or words or letter or letters on the label or other mark, illustration or device, on a package containing any article of food resembling or being an imitation of or being a compound of maple sugar or maple syrup and other substances; and in such cases the exact proportion of maple sugar or maple syrup in such articles shall be clearly indicated on the package.
It will be seen that the makers of maple sugar and maple syrup will be amply protected. The simple indication that the article is composed of maple sugar or maple syrup makes it obligatory that such article shall be pure; and if an article of food is manufactured, containing maple sugar or syrup it is made clear under the amendment that the exact proportion shall be definitely described on the container. I think this will explain the full purpose of the proposed amendment.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways and Canals) Bill No. 71, to authorize an extension of time for the completion of the St. John and Quebec railway between Centreville, in the county of Car-leton, and Andover, in the county of Victoria, N.B., was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-time for construction of line extended.

Has
the minister made any investigation as to

the probable traffic on this road after it is completed? I understood him to say the other day that, when the road was constructed it would be taken over for operation as part of the Canadian Government Railway system and that the Provincial Government that is building the road would he entitled to forty per cent of the gross proceeds as its share of the revenue and the Dominion Government would be entitled to the balance. As I understand the arrangement, the Dominion Government are to undertake the task of operating this railway. I should like to know from the minister if, in his opinion, there is a chance of this road being a profitable one to the Government ralway system.

The agreement with the New Brunswick Government in connection with the operation of this railway was this: The construction of the road was divided into three sections: (a) a railway from Andover, in the county of Victoria, to Centreville, in the county of Carleton, not exceeding twenty-six miles. That part has not been constructed, (b) A railway from Centreville to Gagetown in the county of Queen's, not exceeding one hundred and twenty miles. That part has been completed. (c) A railway from a point at or near Gagetown to a point on the Canadian Pacific railway at or near Westfield in the county of King's, not exceeding forty-five miles. That part has been constructed. In other words, one hundred and sixty-five miles have been constructed and taken over in accordance with the agreement, and that part is being operated by the Canadian National Railways. Nothing has been done in connection with the other portion yet. If the New Brunswick Government should construct it, of course, it would be taken over and operated in the same way as the other.
The information that I have is this: The gross earnings from the two sections that have been completed and taken over were, for the twelve months ended December 31, 1920, $218,127.54; the operating expenses on those two sections for the twelve months ended December 31, 1920, were $564,143.03, leaving an operating deficit of $346,015.49. The above is exclusive of forty per cent of gross earnings payable as rental, amounting to $87,251.01. The hon. member will see that there is a very large operating deficit, and from the information that I have at the present time the deficit in the operation of the road will be very heavy for some
time. This road was built to connect with the Transcontinental running into St. John, making a short line instead of going around by Moncton. It makes the distance a great deal shorter. Whether business will increase as years go by sufficiently to wipe out that operating defiicit, I am not in a position to say.

What
is the total cost of that part of the road which was in operation during 1920?

I am sorry that I have not that information here. It is in Hansard of a year or so ago. If the hon. gentleman wants that information or any other information in that connection, either I can send it to him, or I would have to let the Bill stand. This is merely an extension of time for the construction of that part of the line which has not yet been constructed.
Perhaps the minister can tell us whether this arrangement was profitable to the New Brunswick Government or not.

As I understand the matter, the Provincial Government, even with the share that they get, will lose very heavily-$200,000 or $250,000. The amount they get for their share will not pay the interest on the cost by a very large sum. I am only trusting to my memory as regards the $250,000.
I think it is $220,000.
I thank the hon. gentleman for the information. That is the situation. The Provincial Government loses $220,000, and we lose the amount I have stated.
Is the minister prepared to make a similar arrangement with the other provinces?

I think I can throw some light on the cause of the deficit, both to the province and to the Dominion Government, through this road. When it was first proposed to build this road, as the minister said, it was proposed to build it from St. John to Grand Fails to connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific at Grand Falls, being a short line giving an outlet to the sea through St. John instead of via Moncton. The fact that the section from Andover to Centreville has not been completed and that connection has not been made with the Grand Trunk Pacific is the cause of the deficit largely,

although there may be other contributing causes. The only freight is that which originates on this line, which is to-day only a branch line, whereas it should be part of a through system carrying freight to and from the seaboard. If this short section was completed, or better, if the road was completed on to Grand Palls-if it is not extended to Grand Falls, you will probably have to run from Andover to Grand Falls over the Canadian Pacific-and if a connection was made with the Transcontinental at or near Grand Falls a large quantity of through freight would go over this road to the seaboard and this would no doubt pay, not only the operating expenses of the road to the Dominion, but enough revenue to pay the interest on the bonds out of the forty per cent that goes to the New Brunswick Government as the builder of the road.
I would also like to see the Minister of Railways include, in the arrangement for the subsidy for the building of this road, a subsidy for the building of the connecting link between the St. John and Quebec railway and the Maine Central. Last year a delegation, met the Minister of Railways in Ottawa in order to take this matter up with him. I took the matter up with the minister after the House met this session, and I was told by him that owing to the present railway situation, it was doubtful if any extension work would be done this year. I fully realize the difficulty of carrying on extension work this year under present conditions; but I hope the time will come in the near future when this can be done, and this will make the whole of the Canadian Government Railway system in Eastern Canada a better paying system than it is to-day, from the fact that three-quarters of the freight that originates in eastern Quebec and the Maritime Provinces at the present time is destined for the United States. The Canadian Government system of railways in the Maritime Provinces has no connection with the Maine Central, which is our only outlet to the United States. The Canadian Pacific is the connecting link between the Canadian Government system at St. John and the Maine Central at Vance-boro. What we pay in the course of ten years in excess freight to the Canadian Pacific on this connecting link between St. John and Vanceboro would possibly pay for building the connecting link between the St. John and Quebec railway and the Maine Central which is only 22 miles long and is estimated to cost $1,000,000. We would then have a connecting link of our own to 
the United States. For these reasons, I would strongly urge upon the committee the advisability of the extension proposed by the Minister of Railways in this Bill before the House. It will make it possible for the road to pay not only running expenses but the interest on the bonds as well.

My pur. pose in asking questions was not to oppose the Bill at all, but to try and ascertain whether there was any prospect of the road earning money. I would like to ask the minister whether if any other of the Maritime Provinces makes a proposal to him for the building of a branch line, he would give the same concession with regard to the 40 per cent as he has given in the case of New Brunswick?

Before the minister answers that, I should like to make clear that this is not a branch line. It is the completion of a connecting link between the Intercolonial at St. John and the Grand Trunk Pacific at Grand Falls. Until that is completed, there will be a deficit on the road every year, and I think there is no doubt in the mind of anybody who knows the situation that when the connecting link is completed, not only will the line that it is proposed to build pay, but it will make the whole system there a paying proposition.

My hon. friend is right. This is intended as a connecting link with the Transcontinental. Therefore, it is altogether likely that the Provincial Government will at some future time construct the connecting link, and it will become a part of the Transcontinental system.
Answering the question of my hon. friend from Guysborough, this arrangement was made a number of years ago. As to any future arrangements, each case would have to be considered on its merits. At the present time I would not recommend the construction of any more railways in Canada, because I think we have enough already.

I heard my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton refer to a bonus this Government has to pay, or has paid. I am opposed to bonussing, and I understood the Government has declared against bonussing railways any longer. Would the minister tell us something about this bonus?

Under the arrangement that was made many years ago, this

road received a subsidy from the Dominion Government.
There is nothing more to be paid?

The subsidies have all been paid as the work progressed. When the Canadian Government Railways took over the road, the arrangement was that the province would get 60 per cent of the earnings to pay the interest on the bonds that had been issued for the construction of the railway, and the railway received the other 40 per cent for the cost of operation. That 60 per cent has not proved sufficient to pay the bond interest, which is now $220,000 short.
That, then, is the loss the Government will sustain? It is only a question of the original subsidy.
Oh, no.

Will not the construction of this line divert a certain amount of traffic from the Transcontinental from Grand Falls to St. John? The hon. member for Victoria and Carleton stated that the road would be able to carry itself if this extension were built, but I would think it would result in traffic being diverted from the Transcontinental, and would therefore not be an advantage to the Canadian National Railways.

Of course, the hon.
member knows the country down there much better than I do, I have never been down there. But as I understand the situation, we go from a place called McGivney Junction through to St. John. If this portion were built to Grand Falls it would make the distance shorter than it is from McGivney Junction. We can to-day get to Grand Falls, because we have running rights over the Canadian Pacific. In my judgment, it would be better to do something of that kind rather than parallel another twenty to twenty-five miles of railway. We have a connection now with St. John from McGivney Junction, and we are handling a certain amount of Transcontinental traffic now. It was expected at that time that there would be a lot of traffic from the West that would go through to St. John which would give earnings sufficient to pay not only the operating expenses but the interest on the bonds, but that has not been the case.

I might say in answer to my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) that any freight which
is now diverted from the Grand Trunk Pacific to St. John goes over the Canadian Pacific, so the Canadian National Railways would gain by having their own line to connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific, instead of passing the traffic over to the Canadian Pacific.

Is it the opinion of my
hon. friend that the Transcontinental or the Canadian National Railway should parallel any other line in a territory where there is not sufficient traffic for both?

I might say, in the
first place, that it is not proposed that the Dominion Government build this road. The province will build it, aided by a subsidy from the Dominion Government. The St. John and Quebec railway does not parallel the Canadian Pacific. They come together at Westfield, ten miles out of St. John, and come close together again at Andover. Between Andover and Westfield the territory is well calculated to furnish traffic for both roads. In fact, the proposed route of the St. John and Quebec Railway is through one of the richest farming sections in Eastern Canada, a section absolutely without railway facilities at the present time. This road will not parallel the Canadian Pacific line in any place.

Has the minister an
undertaking with the present owners of this railway that when completed the Government will operate it on the same basis that they are now operating the other portion? Does the minister expect a further loss in operation on that account?

The original agreement includes this part that is to be constructed. Under the agreement, if the Provincial Government decided to construct the 26 miles, the Canadian National Railways will have to operate it, and the result would be a loss. For that reason, I think the Government will hesitate to proceed for a time at least.

Is it a perpetual
agreement, or for a term of years only ?
It is for a long time.
Is it perpetual?
I understand that it is perpetual.

Would not the loss be smaller proportionately if this link were completed? The large contributing factor to the deficit at the present time is the fact that the road does not run to Andover and



connect with the other road at Grand Falls. I know the country very well, and it is contended by everybody that the road cannot pay, stopping where it does at the present time, because it does not tap the best part of the country to get freight.

I have not recently discussed the subject with any of the officials, but some years ago I took the matter up and was informed that the local earnings would not warrant the building of this portion of the road, for the reason that the Canadian Pacific railway runs from Andover, and this road if built would be paralleling it for some twenty miles at least.
I do not think so.

Of course, I am only
speaking from memory on that point. At any rate, I was led to believe that it would not be wise at present to proceed with the construction of that portion. However, that is a question that may be taken up in the future when we know the results of the operation of the 160 miles that we have.

Three surveys have
been made of routes for this proposed road, and one route would parallel the Canadian Pacific railway, the two being on opposite sides of the St. John river. That route, however, was not considered seriously. The western route was taken, and it was considered advisable because it runs a considerable distance away from the Canadian Pacific line and passes through one of the finest sections of Eastern Canada, where a lot of freight would be available. I agree with the Minister of Railways that the local freight does not warrant the building of that portion of the road, but the fact that we would get a lot of through traffic which now goes to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the great possibilities of development in that section, should be a sufficient reason for undertaking the construction. A firm has a charter to develop the electrical power at Grand Falls, the second-best water power in Canada, with a view to building extensive pulp and paper mills. That would provide a large amount of freight destined for the New England states and which would go over the proposed road.

Unquestionably, the extension of this road from Centreville through should be made, and it has occurred to me several times that the minister might well consider the fact that he has had in previous Estimates quite heavy expenditures on the Canada Eastern bridge at Fredericton, 
which it was intended to rebuild and strengthen in order that the heavy traffic off the Grand Trunk Pacific might be diverted from St. John. It is a question his department might well look into, whether it would not pay to make the extension immediately on that line to Andover and through Grand Falls and pick up that freight there, bringing it over the Valley railroad, rather than spend money on the Canada Eastern bridge, on which many thousands of dollars have been expended.

The legislature of New Brunswick has this week passed a resolution calling on the Dominion Government to cancel the outstanding agreement and take over this road, and consolidate it with the Canadian National railways. Is not that a fact?

I did see something to
that effect in the newspapers, but I see nc reason why we should take over a liability of some $220,000 that was created by the province of New Brunswick and should cer tainly be borne by them.
Is there an understanding with the present owners that a subsidy will be paid on this line when constructed? If so, what amount has been agreed to?

The agreement calls
for $6,400 per mile.

In connection with that point, the minister must have misunderstood me or, I misunderstood him. I asked a few moments ago whether the Government had decided to discontinue the pay ment of subsidies, and I understood him to say that no more subsidies would be paid. As I understand now, if this line is constructed, the Government is committed to a payment of $6,400 per mile; and if this charter is not renewed, then the Government is relieved from any responsibility incurred in that connection when the original charter was granted. Now, I believe it is the ayowed policy of the Government not to grant further subsidies to railways. Are we to understand from the minister, if he is in favour of the renewal of this charter, that his object is merely to keep faith with the company in a matter agreed upon some years ago when the original charter was granted? Or are we to understand that the Government have reversed the policy they announced some time ago not to grant further subsidies to railways?

Probably I misunderstood the hon. member. If this
4 p.m. twenty-six miles of railway from Andover to Centreville are con-

structed, under the agreement we shall have to pay the $6,400 per mile. Although this railway is called the St. John and Quebec Railway, it really belongs to the Government of New Brunswick. They built it, put all the money into it, and are responsible for guaranteeing the bonds. The agreement was made practically between the provincial and the Dominion Governments, and I think it would be breaking faith with the province if we refused to extend the charter. There are many reasons why they were not able to proceed with the construction even though they desired to do so. Owing to the war and stress of financial conditions, the proposal had to hang fire, and I do not think it would be fair to the Provincial Government for us to refuse the charter. Their request came to us through the manager- of the road, whose letter I have. It is dated Fredericton, New Brunswick, March 23, and reads:
I am instructed by the hon. Premier Foster, of New Brunswick, and also by the St, John and Quebec Railway Company, to apply to Parliament for an extension of time within which the St. John and Quebec Railway Company may complete construction of its line of railway from Centreville to Andover, until December 31, 1923. This matter is now covered by Act EX, of X George V, chapter 31, and the time expires on December 31, 1921. Similar legislation is being enacted by the province. Will you please advise me whether this will be put through Parliament this season? And oblige,
Tours truly,
W. B. Jones,
President, St. John and Quebec Railway Company.
In extending the time, we are merely keeping faith with the provincial Government.
This is not to be considered a precedent for the revival of the old practice of giving subsidies?

In connection with the question asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Euler), I think the province of New Brunswick would consider it a breach of faith if the Dominion Government refused to renew the subsidy for this portion of the road. I know for a fact that the province would not have undertaken to build that road without an agreement from the Dominion Government that they should receive a subsidy of $6,400 per mile for the *whole distance from St. John to Grand Falls.
When was this agreement made?

I do not know; the minister will be able to tell you. It was previous to the war. . At the time the
137-1*
agreement was entered into, I believe, the Dominion Government agreed to build a bridge across the river at Andover, another bridge across the St. John River, at or near Westville, and another bridge across the Kennebecasis, three very costly bridges on the line, as well as the subsidy of $6,400 per mile on the whole line from St. John to Grand Falls. When the war started, I believe largely due to representations made by the Dominion Government to the province of New Brunswick on account of the war being on, the stringency of the money market, the scarcity of labour, and so forth, the province could not provide for the building of this part of the road at that time which would have meant that the Dominion Government would be compelled to incur large obligations to construct these very costly bridges. The blame is therefore not to be laid on the province of New Brunswick alone for the non-completion of this road. It was generally understood, I am informed, between 'the Dominion Government and Government of New Brunswick that the former should assist towards the building of this road because of the difficulty in financing the undertaking at that time both for the Dominion and the Province, the Dominion then being under the obligation to build the three costly bridges to which I have alluded. Since that time I understand that the obligation by the Dominion to build these bridges has lapsed, and to avoid undertaking expenditures it is now proposed to get connection with the C.P.R. at Westfield Beach and Andover-to obtain running rights over that ten mile section of the Canadian Pacific between these points, and over another twenty mile section of the Canadian Pacific to Grand Falls. Under the circumstances the Dominion Government cannot do less than renew the agreement for subsidizing the twenty-six miles in question.
When was the lease made for the operation of this road?
I think ten or eleven years ago.
Was it a lease to operate?
When the agreement was made with the Province to construct the road it was provided that we were to operate it as part of the Intercolonial system.
Section agreed to. Bill reported, and read the third time and passed.

On the motion of Hon. Hugh Guthrie (Acting Solicitor General) Bill No. 72 to Amend the Winding-up Act was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1-Liquidator to prepare statement of assets and debts.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This Bill is really for statistical purposes. Under section 83 of the present Winding-up Act no time is fixed for- the liquidator to furnish a statement of assets and liabilities. Such is supposed to be almost the first work of a liquidator, but there is no time prescribed in the section as it now stands, and the proposed motion is to allow sixty days to liquidators to prepare a statement of assets, debts, and liabilities.
The section does not say whether the liquidator will have to address such statement to any of the parties concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is in the second clause of the Bill.

The second clause only has reference to the Dominion Statistician. It does not mention the other interested parties. I think there might be an amendment providing for the sending of the statement to the other interested parties.

Section agreed to.
On Section 2-documents to be forwarded to Dominion Statistician.

I would suggest that the minister add a clause providing:
That the liquidator shall, promptly after receipt or preparation, mail to the Dominion Statistician, Bureau of Statistics, Ottawa, and to all the creditors or shareholders a true copy of the following document,

*
And so on.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The liquidator is under the jurisdiction of the court, and in liquidation proceedings, as my hon. friend knows, the court appoints one of its officers and gives direction tu the liquidator as to the winding up of the estate, prescribing what the liquidator shall do, how he shall do it and when he shall do it. I would not like to encumber this clause, which is purely for the purpose of statistical information with any additional requirements which so far are unknown to law.
Section agreed to. Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On the motion of right Hon. Sir George E. Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce) Bill No. 75 concerning the Canadian Wheat Board was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-powers of Wheat Board continued in order that unsettled business may be concluded:

Now I presume my question will be in order, Mr. Chairman. I would again ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce: What opportunity will the holders of outstanding participation tickets have to get them settled before this Wheat Board goes out of business?

It is difficult
to answer that question with reference to some participation tickets that may never be heard of, but the operations of the Board, as my hon. friend knows, ceased at the beginning of the season, and from then up to the present time the work of the Board has been confined to the adjustment of accounts and the payment of the surplus that remained in their hands after the first moiety had been distributed. Every effort is made by the Board itself to call in every participation certificate, and notice now has been out for more than six months. One object-it may be a small part-of having the powers confirmed and continued for a time is to get in all these participation certificates if possible; the other, and main one at the present time, is for the collection of what is overdue and the adjustments that are necessary because of claims and counterclaims in reference thereto.
Will due notice be given in the public press that the Wheat Board is to be wound up so that any parties doing business with it will have a chance to have their certificates settled?

Oh, yes. Six
months ago the Board commenced distributing notices everywhere. I do not know the business of the Board, but from my conversation with Mr. Stewart three weeks ago I should think there are very few participation certificates outstanding that the Board ever expect to have presented, those certificates having been lost or burnt.

I have no
fault to find with the Wheat Board; but of course a few disputes are always likely to arise, and so long as the parties inter-

ested are given a chance to settle their business with the Board it will be quite satisfactory. (

Why is it necessary that
in this Bill we should ratify and confirm all the Orders in Council enumerated? These Orders in Council, I presume, were duly passed, and it seems to me superfluous to ask for their ratification and confirmation.

By those
Orders in Council the powers were conferred upon the Board to do its work, and if you want to continue the Board with its powers-and it must have all its powers because it has not yet finished its business, 

you have to confirm all those different Orders in Council by which those powers were conferred in the first place.
How much has the Wheat Board cost the country, and how much is it going to cost by this continuation? And how is that cost to be met?

The Wheat Board has not cost, and will not have cost, the treasury a single cent when it shall have finished all its business. The whole cost of handling the wheat under the Board has amounted in the whole to a little less than a quarter of a cent per bushel upon the amount handled. The trade itself paid its way, and, as I said, there will probably be a small surplus when all accounts are adjusted.
Is the report of this Board going to be printed-
The report of the Board was laid on the table of the House shortly after the session opened.
The minister did not get my whole question. Is their report going to be printed for distribution?
I do not know. The printing committee have that in charge.
Outside of settling the participation certificates, what unfinished business has the Board to deal with?
The adjustment and collection of outstanding accounts.
How long does the Government propose to keep the Board in operation?
Until it shall have finished its business.
I understand that. But how long does the Government anticipate it will take the Board to finish its business?

I do not know, but from the conversation I had with the chairman of the Board I understand that less than three months from the first of March would see the end of the outstanding business. Of course, you can never tell -sometimes lawyers get mixed up with these claims.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, and read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
That it is expedient to provide that the time for the payment of the debentures amounting to two million dollars, issued by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal to His Majesty under chapter ten of the statutes of 1896, entitled, "An Act respecting the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal," be extended to the first day of July, 1946 ; and that the time for the payment of the debentures amounting to two million dollars, issued by the said Commissioners to His Majesty under the authority of chapter forty-seven of the statutes of 1898, entitled "An Act to grant further aid to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal," be extended to the first day of July, W51.
Will the minister explain why this extension is necessary?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The capital moneys required by the port of Montreal were supplied by the issue of these debentures. The Harbour Commission pays interest on the debentures, but the debt itself is of a permanent nature. It is proposed to extend to 1946 $2,000,000 of these debentures falling due this year, and to 1951 $2,000,000 falling due in four years' time. Of course, payment of the principal will no more be thought of on the dates mentioned than it is now, but this procedure is better for the Harbour Commission, who do not wish to show past-due liabilities on their books. The matter will be treated, as it now is, as a permanent investment.
This is really a loan to the harbour commissioners and for nominal security they deposit these debentures. Is it proposed to issue new debentures, or is it simply the extension of the old ones?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Simply to extend the old ones.
The interest is payable to the Dominion Government?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is the renewal at the rate of the original issue? What is the rate of interest?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I remember rightly, it is five per cent. The interest is paid up from year to year; there is nothing overdue. At least, if there is anything overdue it has been but for a short time.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 77, to extend the time for the payment of certain debentures issued by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Dealing with the last point first, the penalty, I presume, will be set forth in the Bill which my'hon. friend proposes to introduce?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I entirely commend my hon. friend for giving Canada a new coin. The matter has been discussed from time to time. It was discussed last session, and I then very cordially supported the suggestion that we should have a nickel coin. Has my hon. friend yet reached any conclusion as to the design of the coin?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The design
has not yet been selected. The only conclusion we have come to is as to the size and weight. The new coin will be of the standard weight of 70 grains, and will be of exactly the same size as the American coin.

It has not heretofore been found necessary in Canada to have any legislation concerning the melting down or breaking up of gold coins. One could hardly conceive that it would make gold any more valuable to break it up, but as a matter of fact, it was found during
the war that gold in the form of bullion was worth more than in the form of coin and there were several prosecutions in England, under the law my hon. friend has referred to, for melting down gold coin. I think he has been quite wise in adopting the provisions of the English Act in that respect.
One of the possible objections to a nickel coinage is the colour; one is likely to confuse nickel with silver. That has even been noticeable in France, where the white metal comes into competition with silver. That is sometimes embarrassing, and if we could avoid it by having a different-sized coin, that would be very helpful. My hon. friend has given us a new cent. It was constructed, I believe, on grounds of economy, which I ought to commend-he has put as little copper in the cent as possible. He must have designed it, I think, at a time when copper was 30 cents a pound. Now it is worth 12 cents a pound, and I think my hon. friend is trying to make a great deal more money out of that one-cent piece than is necessary or wise.
There is another difficulty. In handling coinage, the sense of touch is of great assistance. When a man puts his hand in his pocket, he likes to be able to tell by his sense of touch which coin he is drawing out, but my hon. friend's new one-cent piece is so near the size of the ten-cent piece that sometimes it is a little embarrassing. I am told, and I have seen it in the press, that taking advantage of that similarity in size some shrewd and not too honest persons have silvered over the Canadian cent and have succeeded occasionally in passing it off as a ten cent piece. I could wish, for that reason, that in the selection of the one-cent piece the hon. gentleman had not been so economical, but had made it a little larger than the ten-cent piece. I have the two in my hand at the moment, and while there is a perceptible difference when one's attention is drawn to it, the difference is very slight. I think it is a pity for that reason that we did not get a little larger cent. When you put your hand in your pocket for a couple of cents for a newspaper, very often you will find you are drawing out a ten-cent piece. One is as likely to come out as the other, the difference is so very slight. That, however, is only a mild form of criticism but if the hon. gentleman has at another time occasion to make a new design or to reconsider the size of the one-cent piece, I think the point would be well worth considering. With the main purpose of the resolution, as
regards the nickel coinage, I am very heartily in accord.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman is quite right as to economy being a factor in the size of the new one-cent piece. Perhaps what we had most in mind was to save the lining of the pockets of my hon. friend from Beauce, who complained that the larger cent wore his pockets out, and he made a heart-rending appeal for a smaller coin. I hope he likes it. I quite appreciate the point made by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), but there are many difficulties connected with it. For example, the old cent was very near the size of a quarter, and people used to pull out of their pockets a quarter when they wanted a cent, and vice versa. I think the point my hon. friend makes as to the sense of touch is important. Of course, there is no milling on the cent, as there is on the ten-cent piece. There will be no milling on the nickel. I would be very much pleased if the hon. gentleman would be so kind as to come into the office and look over the blanks with me and give me the benefit of his advice.
I think I can trust the hon. gentleman to do that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I beg to move that the word "five" be substituted for the word "ten" in the second line of paragraph two of the resolution.

House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
. Mines and Geological Survey: For organization and equipment of the Explosive Division, under the Explosives Act, Chap. 31, 4-5 George Y, $11,500.

What does
this branch do?

This Explosives division was created in 1919 to administer the Explosives Act, passed previously. The duties of the officials are to draw up and enforce regulations for the manufacture, storage, importation, sale, and use of all explosives, to inspect factories and magazines, to issue licenses for the same, and to work in co-operation with the provincial

and Dominion police. The staff comprises, one chief inspector, two chemists, one inspector, and two clerks. There is a decrease in the vote this year, due to the fact that some of the staff have been placed on the permanent list.

Item agreed to.
Mines Branch, $272,100.
This is practically the same in all particulars as the vote of last year?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Geological Survey, $332,000.

What is reputed to be a great oil find has been made in the Mackenzie district, and I think it would be well for the minister to make a general statement in regard to the Government's policy concerning, say, a wireless telegraphy system in connection with that district, the question as to how the staffs of the Geological Department are to be transported, the construction of a pipe line in that district if oil is found in sufficient quantity, and so on. The people throughout Canada are very much interested in this discovery, and a statement from the minister would be advisable.

This comes ' under the Department of Interior, and will be dealt with when the Estimates of that department are under consideration. I have made a note of the hon. member's suggestion and shall be glad to make the statement he asks for.

The minister, in answer to a question last evening, said that the department were sending a number of parties from the Geological division into that district. I wanted to know how they were to be transported, and he said by canoes. Great exception is taken to this means of transportation by the men in the field, who think it is a mistake not to have these parties transported by aeroplane. Transportation by canoes does not make for expedition, which is essential in matters of this kind.

It was the intention of
the Air Board to take up the proposition of air transportation to this area, but the Estimates of that board were reduced, and they are, therefore, unable to consider the question this year. There will be
5 p.m. no loss of time in transportation; the men are on their way now,

and will be on the ground as soon as it is ready for operations.
How long does it take to make the trip from Edmonton to Port Norman?
From two to three weeks.
Do these parties operate from Port Norman or any particular district?
They carry on explorations between Great Slave lake and Fort Good Hope.

I notice an item of
$1,500 for museum equipment. This seems to be a standing vote every year. What is it for?	.

It is for necessary equipment for the museum in Ottawa. This is under the Mines Branch, and the money is for the purpose of building cases for exhibits, providing for the purchase and storage of specimens, and occasional purchases of collections of minerals, Indian handicraft, skins of animals, etc., and also for purposes of research in the museum.
Is this an annual expenditure? It seems to be a fixed charge.

This appropriation has
been made for the last two years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

What are the duties of
the junior purchasing agent in this department? On page 101, giving the details of these Estimates, provision is made for this official of $1,770.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
From what page is
the hon. member reading?
Page 101.
That item was carried last night and therefore the question is not in order.

The hon. member will
find a full explanation in Hansard of to-day.
Referring to the Geological Survey Department-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item has been declared carried.
Well, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) got the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not want to
interfere with any legitimate discussion -I do not think that the Chairman should
do so. On the other hand it is not in order for hon. members to retain their seats until long after a motion has been declared carried and then ask to refer to it again. However, if the hon. member (Mr. Johnston) did not hear the Chairman's declaration,
I think his question should be allowed if it is relevant.

My question is, just what parties are going into this district?
I think the minister said there were five.
No, four.
How many individuals are there in each party and who is the head of each party?

There are five men in
each party, and the heads of the parties are Dr. Williams, Dr. Hume, Mr. Whittaker and Mr. Dowling. .
Is item 250, Geological Survey, still open for consideration?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

I find two objects of this item to be for the purchase of specimens for the Victoria Museum, and for publications of English and French editions of reports, maps and illustrations. Are these purchases made through the Purchasing Commission, or are they made by the junior purchasing agent, or by the senior purchasing agent?
Every purchase is made by the Purchasing Commission. We have no senior purchasing agent; the official is classified as "junior purchasing agent" by the Civil Service Commission.
How are the reports of these field parties transmitted to Ottawa?
The reports come in in the fall.
That is to say, reports of the work they are doing from now until the fall months will not be available at the offices here until the autumn of the present year.
That is the procedure as regards these outlying districts.

I notice an item of $197,000 for explorations, surveys, investigations, and so on. I presume that would also apply to investigations in the Fort Norman oil field, as it is called. Now the public of Canada are very much interested in the possibilities of that field. So far as regards

the development that has gone on I think the only results have been obtained by the Imperial Oil Company of Canada; but in view of the fact that a good many oil companies are being formed and that appeals are being made to the public to take stock in these companies, I would ask the minister whether the Government itself, or the Department of Mines, is making any effort to establish the extent of the oil fields, and whether any information will be given to the public that would serve as a guide for them in connection with the activities of oil promoters in the flotation of companies?

I may say that a general survey of the district was made about thirty years ago by Mr. McConnell of the Geological Survey Department; he remained in there two summers and one winter making general surveys of the whole Mackenzie river basin. The object of the four parties that are going into that district at the present time is to carry out that work in detail and to secure information that will be of value to the development of that particular district.
Will the field be left entirely to private explorers, or is the Government drilling for oil?

We do not do any drilling; we simply carry on a geological survey of the country. The drilling will be done by private parties under the regulations that have been framed for that par-, ticular section of the country.
Does the department propose to supply to the general public any information with regard to the possibilities of that oil field?
Every bit of the information obtained by the parties sent out by the Government is available to the public.
Will the minister explain the nature of the surveys that are being made?
It is a survey of the geology and the general structure of the country so as to be of use in prospecting for oil.

This is a most important matter, and I would ask the minister how" this information will be made available to the public. Out West we expect a very large oil boom in that country this year. We had an oil boom in Calgary some time ago but it was a fake-in fact CM.r. Euler.]
there was more hot air than oil about it- and a great many people lost their money owing to the activities of exploiters. There should be something done in this case to get the information to the public as quickly as possible as to whether or not there is a genuine field for investment.

Our inspector will be visiting the district in August with a view to securing information from these parties which he will impart to the public, and final reports will come in when the parties have completed their surveys for the season.
What system is employed in order to get this information out to the public?
The information is sent out through the newspapers, and later on when the final reports come in they are available to the public.
Will the Department of Mines issue bulletins containing information on the subject?
That is done regularly where it is considered important.

Is there any
definite information now in regard to the oil flow at Fort Norman?
Not first-hand information.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, $3,000.
This is the customary grant is it not?

This is the annual grant to the Canadian Mining Institute, which is a technical society organized in the interests of the mining industry of Canada. This amount has been voted annually for over twenty years, with a view to defraying the cost of public information regarding the mineral resources and mining conditions of the country.
Is it an association of mining engineers?
Mining engineers and prospectors.	.

Item agreed to.
Grant to Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau $12,166.67.
This is one item upon which I desire to have some explanation.

I desire, Mr. Chairman, to renew the protest which I made last year in regard to this item. The mineral resources of Canada as well as our other natural resources are Canadian resources. Why should any of our resources be called Imperial resources? I believe in the British Empire, but our property is Canadian property. What is the purpose of that Bureau? Was Parliament consulted before its creation?

This Bureau was created in 1917 in London. The Prime Minister, I understand, was present at the opening meeting. As I have pointed out, the Bureau is for the purpose of all the British Dominions joining together with a view to advertising their mineral resources and gathering information as to the supplies of minerals in different parts of the British Empire, with a view to making the British Empire independent so far as mineral supplies are concerned. I am quite sure that this Bureau, conducted as it is and with the meetings that they hold from time to time, will render great service to the development of the mineral resources of this country and to the men interested in them.
In what way can Canada benefit from the work of that Bureau?
What kind of advertising? Where does this advertising take place?
Advertising in the greatest centre of capital in the world-right in the city of London.
I do not think Canada needs any advertising in London. Surely the minister does not pretend that we must do anything to advertise our resources in London?
We are busy advertising cur agricultural resources there all the time, and with very great benefit to the agriculturists of this country.
What is the nature of the undertaking as between the different overseas nations in connection with this Bureau? What kind of bargain have we gone into there? Is it to be perpetual?

To whom is this bureau
responsible?
To a board of governors, and each of the Dominions is represented on that board.
Who represents Canada? Mr. TOLMIE: Dr. Miller, of Toronto.

Has a report of this
bureau been presented to this House?

The first report is not
available yet, but it will be presented as soon as it is ready.

As the first report since 1917 is not yet available, I do not see much sense in spending further money on this bureau. At any rate I think the minister might pass the item over for the present until we get further information. We are getting entangled in all kinds of affairs without our knowledge. I have no recollection of this item being passed last year, although, of course, that is no reason for thinking that it was not passed regularly. But we were told the other night about a board being organized after we had battled in the House against its organization and the proposition had been withdrawn on two occasions. But the board was established by Order in Council and we were told that we are responsible for it.
This money was voted for the first time last year. Would the hon. gentleman like to have any further information?
I would like to have the report.
We will be very glad to send him one as soon as it is available. Although the establishment of the bureau was agreed to in 1917, our first contribution to it was not made until last year.
Was the same amount expended last year?
Yes.
Where did it go? Who got it?
It was transferred to the bureau as our contribution. I cannot give details of the expenditure at the present time.

I do not think it is very
good business'that we should be asked to transfer $12,000 or any other sum to a" bureau that we know nothing about. We have no report of its activities nor any information of how our contribution was expended or what benefit accrued to us. I think we should have more details.

I would like to ask my hon. friends opposite who are objecting to 
this item if they have failed to recognize this point? Canada has a very wide diversity of resources, particularly mineral. Some of the minerals are somewhat rare and are needed in Great Britain, we will say, or in some other part of the Empire. As I understand it, remembering last year's presentation of this matter, this bureau is for the purpose of familiarizing the Empire with the resources available in its different parts. I remember very distinctly the impression I got at the time that this was an exceedingly useful institution for Canada, as we have perhaps more of these resources than any other part of the Empire, and what we are doing is bringing the attention of the friendly sister Dominions and of the Mother Country to those resources so that they may secure them here rather than in foreign countries. I submit to the committee that this bureau is a very desirable institution, and while its first report is not yet in, I do not think we should object to the item without very serious consideration of that feature.

In answer to the hon.
member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) all I have to say is that we do not know what we are doing-no report has been submitted-and just because the hon. member gets up and tells us that this is something of considerable importance is no reason why we should accept his view. Indeed, his own opinion is discounted because he does not know anything about the report itself. He is asking this committee to pass a vote for something that he says must be right because some one else said so last year. That is not the way to do the business of this House.

My hon. friend is
altogether overheated in his response. I simply invited attention to a feature which I thought was useful and of great benefit to Canada.

The suggested usefulness may be all right; that is what we want to find out. We want to know what our money is being spent for; who is spending it; to whom this committee are reporting; and when we may get a statement of the expenditure. We have no money to throw away in making soft jobs for people. We have enough soft-job holders in this country without going outside to provide places for them. If the minister is not prepared to give a report, I think he should let the matter stand until he is in a position to do so.
Carried.
No, it is not carried. If my hon. friend wants to carry it, he knows how to do so. If he has not enough courtesy to wait for the minister to answer we will teach it to him right here and now.

I may say that the report is not available as yet, but we can likely furnish in a few days the details of how this money has been expended. If the committee desires it, I am quite willing to let this item stand until such time as I am able to produce the information.
Item stands.
Miscellaneous-to provide for expenses in connection with a Canadian exhibit at the National Exposition of Chemical Industries, New York.
Do we spend money every year on this exposition?
We are exhibiting now for the first time.
Then what was the amount of $7,500 spent for last year?
That was for the purchase of material and specimens for the exhibition of this year; also for the purchase of space.

Item agreed to.
Civil Government-Indian Affairs-salaries, $142,735 ; contingencies, $19,000.
What has been done by the Department under the law passed last year providing for the compulsory enfranchisement of the Indians?
No action has been taken yet with reference to compulsory enfranchisement; no officials have been appointed to carry on the work.
To what does the minister attribute the reports in the press that the Six Nation Indians are going across the border into the United States?
That is an unfounded rumour, so far as I am aware. I cannot account for the action of the newspapers in matters of that kind; it would be very difficult to keep track of some of them.

The actions of the Government have been such that any one seeing newspaper reports of that kind would naturally have his suspicions aroused. The Government did bring in a Bill and it is not surprising for any one to expect drastic action at any time.

The committee which considered the Bill, to which I have just referred, made a report in which it was
suggested that a standing committee of this House should be appointed in regard to Indian Affairs. Is it the intention of the minister to take such a step?
It has not been considered, so far as I am aware.
What is the salary of the Indian Commissioner at Regina? If there has been an increase in his salary, when and upon whose recommendation was it made?

The present Indian
Commissioner there receives $4,800 a year. His salary was increased from $3,600, and the action was taken by the Civil Service Commission.
Are all these appointments made through the Civil Service Commission?
Yes.
When did this increase become effective?
Last year; I could not give the exact date.
Has the Civil Service Commission power to fix and increase salaries, or must that be done in accordance with the reclassification?

It must be done in
accordance with their reclassification and in the carrying out of the Act.
I see there is a new official to be appointed, an assistant senior engineer. What are his duties?
He takes care of the roads, bridges, ditching and other works of an engineering character on the Indian Reserves.

I see there is a salary of $3,000 for the private secretary to the minister. The Minister of Indian Affairs, I understand, is also Minister of the Interior. Has he a private secretary for each of these Departments?
Yes.
Is the Indian Commissioner at Regina given an allowance by way of residence, or does the amount of salary stated by the minister constitute his whole remuneration?
He receives a free house in addition to his salary.

Has Sir James Loug-heed not a department to supervise apart

from the Department of the Interior and the Department of Indian Affairs?
Interior, Indian Affairs and Mines, also Civil Re-establishment and Soldiers' Land Settlement.
Has he a private secretary for each of the departments?
He has one for the Department of the Interior and one for the Department of Indian Affairs, but not one for each of the other departments.

Perhaps the minister would give the committee a short review of the Indian situation in Canada, giving the number of reserves and the location and population of each reserve. It would also be most interesting to know whether the Indian population in Canada is increasing or decreasing, and to what extent.

There is practically no change in the number of Indian reserves. There are about three hundred reserves. The Indian population, about 100,000, is just about the same. I do not think it is necessary for me to go into the full details. All that can be obtained in the report of the Department of Indian Affairs.
All I wanted was a general statement of that character. I am glad to know the Indian population in Canada, also the number of reserves. In what province are the reserves mainly located?
The greatest number are located in British Columbia; there are a number in Saskatchewan, Alberta and the other provinces.
Are there any reserves in Quebec?
About thirty.

The Indians at Riviere du Loup in the county of Temiscouata have been deprived of the services of their doctor, Dr. Lebel, who has moved to the West. I do not think any nomination has yet been made. When will a doctor be appointed for the tribe in the county of Temiscouata?
This matter is now in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. As soon as we receive their decision, we shall have a man to attend to those Indians.

Speculators are after some lands in Temiscouata that belong to the Indians, spruce lands, very good lands. Orders were given by the department to

sell this land. The Indians called on me one day and protested against this. I wrote to the department, and at the time the agent had received orders to sell the land. The deputy minister told me at the time that the order was put aside for a while. Will this order stand good forever, or what is the intention of the department in regard to this land?

It is not the intention
of the department to sell those lands immediately, and the order will, I suppose, stand until such time as conditions change so as to indicate the necessity of some other course.

The minister informed the committee that the salary of the Indian commissioner at Regina had been increased from $3,600 to $4,800 within the last year upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission. Have all other employees of the Indian Department received similar increases?

No, the other employees of the department did not receive any increase in salary. This man, whom I have met, is thoroughly versed in Indian affairs, a very valuable man. I remember last year, at the opening of the Regina exhibition, viewing an Indian agricultural exhibit that would have been a credit at any show anywhere. This was shown to me with great pride by this particular man and it had been worked up by him. If he was doing work such as this exhibit indicated, it would seem as if he was worth this salary.

Two sessions ago I was told by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) that it was in his mind to remove the agency of the Indians in Temiscouata county from Cacouna to Riviere du Loup. There are practicaly no Indians at Cacouna; they are all in the vicinity of Riviere du Loup. The Indian agent, Mr. Lebel, is an old man over seventy, a wealthy man, and when the Indians want something, they have to make a trip down to Cacouna, or telephone. I was promised at the time that the matter would be looked into and that, perhaps, the agency would be moved from Cacouna to Riviere du Loup. Has any progress been made in that connection?

The matter was investigated by the Indian Department, but they did not decide to move the agency to Riviere du Loup. The matter is not, however, be-

yond being changed, and I shall be very glad to bring it to the attention of the minister in charge.
Has the Indian commissioner at Regina a free residence? Is that residence owned by the department?
Yes.
When was it purchased? How long has he had the use of that place and what was the price paid for it?

The agent has had the use of a residence, the rent of which was paid by the department until two years ago, when it was considered better to purchase a new residence for him. This residence was purchased at a price of $12,500 two years ago, and he has occupied that residence since.
From whom was this residence purchased?
I regret that I am unable to give the name of the vendor.

The reference made by the minister to the exhibit by Indians at the Regina exhibition reminds me that, at various times when distinguished visitors have come to Canada from overseas, it has been the custom of some department-I do not know whether it is the Department of State which takes care of these visitors or whether this custom has been initiated by the Department of Indian Affairs-to bring the Indians in from away back on the reserves to stations along the line in order to show them to these visitors. That was particularly noticeable during the recent press conference that was held in this country in August last. It just so happened that at that time I was in England, from reading the English newspapers one would get the idea that the only thing we had to show in Canada was Indians. The papers from day to day were telling how these Indians came down to meet the distinguished visitors, who seemed to be more delighted and impressed with the visit of the Indians than any other feature of Canadian life. I do not object to having the Indians pay their respects, but it seems to me that the next time there are distinguished visitors in this country, it would be well for us to impress them with the idea that we have something more than Indians to show.

The policy of the department is entirely opposed to the practice to which my hon. friend has referred. We do
not organize these visits of Indians to meet visitors to Canada. I had a very striking-illustration of that two years ago, at the time of the big cowboy round-up in Calgary, when the department was requested to let the Indians go out there to add picturesqueness to the scene. I know the department absolutely refused to let them go, but I do not think there was an Indian within a thousand miles of Calgary who had a horse that could carry him who was not there.
What is the nature of these exhibits?
An exhibit of grains, roots, and general field produce. It was a very excellent exhibit, and a large one too.

I have another question regarding the increase in salary to the Indian Commissioner at Regina. The minister stated that the increase was made upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission. I understand that we had an American firm in this country investigating and reporting on our Civil Service, and I would like to know if this increase was made on their recommendation, and if the Indian Department was investigated by that organization.

The American organization confined their work largely to the city of Ottawa. They had nothing to do with the recommendation of this particular increase. It was recommended by the Civil Service Commission.
Was the increase made through the reclassification?
Yes.
Might we have an idea as to what his duties were before reclassification?
Before reclassification he was inspector for South Saskatchewan. His duties have been considerably enlarged, and he is now' Indian Commissioner.
What does the enlargement of hjs duties consist of?

Previously his duties
were confined to the inspection of reserves in South Saskatchewan. His field has been increased so that he now looks after the whole of the three Prairie Provinces.
Does he give any more time to the work than he did before?
Very much more.
I understood that he Mr. TOLMIE:	That is the usual allowwas a permanent officer before. Is he now ance for the private secretary. That is a super-permanent officer? Or what? done in all departments.
More efficient, I would say.
What are the duties of the supervisor of Indian timber lands?
His business is to inspect and place valuation on timber for sale on the reserves, and also to insist in fire protection.
Has he supervision over all the reserves in Canada?
He is available for work in any part of Canada, where he may be directed to go by headquarters.
How is the sale of timber-lands carried on? Is the timber sold on the report of some individual?
By public auction, or by tender after having been thoroughly advertised.

Do you have to get the sent of the Indians?
con-
Yes, in the usual way.

There are
two inspectors of Indian Agencies. That would seem to indicate a new appointment. What is the necessity for another inspector?
One is inspector for northern Alberta and the Peace River District, and the other inspector for Ontario and Quebec.

Are there
two inspectors at present?

These two have come
under civil government. There are more inspectors in the Outside Service, which we will come to later.
There is only one inspector at the present time, is there not?

There is one permanent
officer, but the other one has been transferred from the Outside Service, and now comes under civil government.

Coming back to the
question of private secretary, I notice that apart from his salary of $3,000 an allowance of $600 is provided on the same page for private secretary. Does the allowance go to the same officer?

What is the necessity
for that extra allowance? Does he receive that in addition to the bonus?

If he were entitled to
receive the bonus, he would receive it. This allowance of $600 is granted to all the private secretaries on account of the overtime they have to put in. My own private secretary-I can only give my own experience-is frequently working overtime; he is sometimes in this building until midnight and past, and often works on Sundays and Saturday afternoons. I presume this allowance is to meet that situation.

Why is it not given in
one lump sum with the salary? I notice that all the private secretaries get this allowance of $600, in the Indian Affairs Department, for instance, Mines Department, Interior Department, Soldiers' Land Settlement, and so on. But why is it not given as part of the salary?

A private secretary
might be taken out of the ranks of the Civil Service, and this $600 allowance is some compensation for the extra time he has to put in as private secretary. If he returns to the ranks, the allowance is stopped.

I notice we are
asked to vote a salary of $5,600 for chief of party. I would like to know what the duties of this officer are, and whether the item refers to Mr. Bain, the new organizer of the National Liberal and Conservative party.
This refers to two men at $2,800 each, chiefs of parties who carry on survey work on the Indian reserves.

What are
the names of these inspectors of Indian agencies?
H. A. Conroy and C. C. Parker.
Which of them is in the Inside Service now?

Conroy has been for some time. As a matter of fact, they are both in the Inside Service now.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; This item, as represented here, would indicate a new appointment beginning with the new year.
They are both in the Inside Service now, but this is the first time the other has been estimated for the Inside. The estimate for last year was different.
Why are some of these inspectors in the Inside Service and some in the Outside? What is the particular reason for bringing this officer into the Inside Service?
He has always been stationed in Ottawa. His duties have lain in eastern Ontario and Quebec, and he has always been stationed here.
Why was he not in the Inside Service before?

I canot say; I did not become Acting Minister of Interior until a short time ago.
