Indians, Ontario and Quebec, $142,135.
There is an increase of $36,860 in this item. Will the minister explain the reason for it?

The increase is due in part to the transfer from the Estimates for the province of Manitoba to the Estimates for the province of Ontario of the
items relating to the Fort Frances and Kenora agencies amounting to $13,018. Formerly these items were included in the Manitoba Estimates, but as these agencies are located in Ontario it is considered that a change should now be made and they are accordingly incorporated in the Estimates for the province of Ontario. This change is also in line with a suggestion from the Auditor General's Department. A corresponding reduction is made in the Manitoba Estimates. The balance of the increase, $750, is due to the increase of salaries granted under classification of the service.
What about the increase of $15,018 for medical attendance and medicine?

The balance of the increase is explained by the transfer of the Estimates of the Fort Frances, Kenora, and Savanne agencies which were formerly included in the Manitoba Estimates but are now transferred to the Ontario Estimates where they properly belong. There will be a corresponding reduction in the Manitoba Estimates so that on the whole there will be no increase. This Estimate is to cover the cost of administration both in Ontario and Quebec.

The minister will notice that there is an increase in the Estimates for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories amounting to $17,796, so that the corresponding reduction, of which he speaks, is not apparent.
I will be very glad to explain that when we get to the Estimates for Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

The reason I mention it now is because the minister says there is a corresponding reduction in the Estimates for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, whereas all these grouped together show that instead of a reduction there is an increase of over $17,000.
There is a reduction, but on other items there has been an increase in those provinces which I will be very glad to explain when we get the items themselves.

Item agreed to.
Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, $574,210.

I understand that certain lands in the Muscowegan reserve in



Saskatchewan have been surrendered by the Indians at the request of certain residents of that district. Are those lands to be surveyed, subdivided and placed on the market this year?
This land is covered by a lease at present, but as soon as arrangements can be made for its termination the land will be placed on the market.
When will that lease expire?
It does not expire until 1923, but negotiations are now proceeding for its termination.
Does not that lease carry a clause for cancellation?
There was no clause for cancellation in that particular lease.
Why not?
It was left out. Just why I am unable to say at the present moment.
Who drew the lease?
It was drawn by the Indian Commissioner.
With regard to the land that has been taken out of the Riding Mountain reserve in Manitoba, has any provision been made to reimburse the Indians?
Yes, they will be reimbursed.
To what extent?
That has not been settled yet.
What is the basis of the arrangement? It is not very satisfactory to be told that the matter will be settled.
I will give the hon. gentleman the information as soon as I get it.
We want it now.
He will get it now. The land has not yet been surrendered, Mr. Chairman, and we are unable to give particulars until the change takes place.
Has the minister any idea of what arrangements are being made? Are the Indians giving their consent?

No. Negotiations are
actually in progress at the present time. In the event of a satisfactory arrangement being concluded, the Indians will either be reimbursed in cash or Other land.

In connection with the land in the Muscowegan reserve the department, as I understand it, were requested by a number of returned men in that district to open it for settlement. The department acted also for another reason, that this reserve was right up against a certain town and the residents were not able to get sufficient land into their school district to carry on. Now from the minister's reply to my previous question, I would gather that were it not for the fact that this lease does not carry a cancellation clause the land would be open immediately. I should like to place on the right individual the responsibility for not having chat cancellation clause in the lease. Who was responsible for that omission?
The Indian Commissioner issued the lease, and of course that is the reason why it cannot be cancelled at the present time.
It is a fact that leases ordinarily carry a cancellation clause?
Yes, that is the fact.
Who holds this lease?
A Mr. White.
What is the reason for the increase in the item under the heading General Expenses? Last year the estimate was $259,006; this year it is $281,445.

This is due to increases in salaries granted under classification of the service from first of April 1919 to first of April 1921, amounting to $26,160, and to increases which may be granted for the fiscal year 1921-1922 amounting to $6,680, making a total of $32,840, From this total should be deducted $10,401, representing the Estimates of the Fort Frances and Ken-ora agencies, which are situated in Ontario. These formerly were included in the Estimates of Manitoba, but are now transferred to the Estimates of Ontario, where they properly belong. There will be a corresponding increase in the Ontario Estimates The net increase therefore amounts to $22,439 in the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta Estimates.
Does this vote carry an amount for a new school building on the Gordon reserve, Saskatchewan?
That will be under the vote for Indian education which we will reach very shortly.

The minister stated that he would explain the difference in Manitoba

when he came to the Saskatchewan Estimates. The Saskatchewan Estimates show two items of decrease amounting to $8,000. Is that where he gets the $36,000 increase in the Ontario and Quebec items?

As I explained, Mr. Chairman, from this total of $32,000 should be deducted the sum of $10,401 representing the Estimates of the Fort Frances and Ken-ora agencies, which are situated in Ontario and which have formerly been included in the Estimates of Manitoba, but are now transferred to the Estimates of Ontario where they properly belong. There will be a corresponding increase in the Ontario Estimates. The net increase therefore amounts to $22,439 in the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta Estimates.
Have the salaries of Indian agents been increased?

Yes, in amounts varying from $200 to $600, according to the Civil Service classification.
Indians-Nova Scotia, $50,140.

Has the amount spent on the Indians in Nova Scotia encouraged them in any way? Are the farms more productive than they have been in the past? The minister knows that large areas are occupied by the Indians in several portions of the province.
The Indians have, on the whole, been rather backward in Nova Scotia in agriculture, but a slight improvement has been noticed in late years.
There is an item for roads; will the minister tell us where this money is being expended?
The amounts have not yet been allotted, but the expenditure is usually made on the request of the Indian agents, for improvements to roads in the various agencies.
What amount of the item "miscellaneous and unforeseen" was expended last year?

This is for the removal of Indians from Sydney reserve to a new location. The location of the new reserve has not yet been settled; therefore the money has not been expended. It is re-voted this year for the purpose.
Indians-New Brunswick, $23,784.
Will the minister explain the increase?

$1,200 for increase of
agents' salaries under the classification and $300 increase granted to doctors for part time service.
Who is the Indian superintendent in the north shore district of New Brunswick?
Mr. Sheridan.

I understand that Mr. Sheridan resigned his position last year to become a candidate in the provincial election held in October. He appears, however, to be still filling the position. I cannot understand how he could have been a candidate in that election and still be acting in the capacity of Indian superintendent without being re-appointed. I observe that an increase of salary is provided for here; surely that is not on his account.

It was to make up his
election expenses-he lost his deposit.

That is entirely new to
me. I will give the hon. member information in the matter. I am sorry I cannot do it just now.

This is a somewhat important statement that should not be passed over lightly. If officers of the Crown are to take part in elections-become candidates, apparently-there is a different rule in the Indian Department from that which applies in the Department of Railways, where Mr. Hanna has issued instructions that the railway employees are not to take any part in elections. It seems to me that the minister should give a more explicit reply to my hon. friend in that respect.

I quite agree that this
does seem to be a case where more information is necessary; that is why I do not assume the responsibility of replying definitely to my hon. friend now. I would rather have an opportunity to give a full reply in this matter.
Perhaps the minister would be willing to let the item stand in the meantime?

I shall be glad to do that. Mr. CALDWELL:	How many Indian
agents are on salary in New Brunswick? Mr. TOLMIE: Three.
Item allowed to stand.
Indians-Prince Edward Island, $3,935.

How many Indians are
there in Prince Edward Island?

292.

Indians-'general, $192,000.

I notice there is an increase in general expenses of fifty per cent, whereas in the item for education the increase is only twenty per cent. Will the minister explain the large increase for general expenses?

This increase is required in connection with the payment of Indians surrendering their lands under the provisions of section 89 of the Indian Act, which will be repaid from the avails of the land. It is necessary to ask for an increased vote in view of the expectations of Indian Commissioner Graham that he will be able to secure in the next fiscal year surrenders from Indians and it will require this extra sum to make the advances to the Indians interested. This will be regarded simply as a loan to be repaid as soon as the lands are sold, which will probably be within a year or two.
Does the minister anticipate any profit in respect'of these transactions?

A profit may often be
secured, but if so it reverts to the Indians.

The question I
asked with regard to the new school to be built on the Gordon reserve would come under this item, I suppose. Is there an amount in this vote for that school?
Yes, a portion of the vote is appropriated for that school.

maintenance and repairs to wharves; $10,000.

To provide for breaking ice in Thunder Bay, Lake Superior, and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000.

In what manner does
the minister intend to provide for breaking ice in Thunder Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For the first time in the history of the Marine Department, during the past winter there was no ice to speak of to break. A powerful tug and some other boats are kept constantly at Fort William for the purpose of breaking up the ice Whenever it forms. We have a contract that the firm shall do that work for $40,000 a year.
Am I to understand that this firm is paid $40,000 a year whether there is any work for it to do or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is perfectly right; but as he is just as familiar with Port Arthur and Fort William as I am, he will understand that that is rather a cold part of the country; that there is always ice, and thick ice, in that region. This last winter was an exceptional winter as my hon. friend knows. Therefore, the ice was quite thin, and the work entailed in breaking it up was nothing like what it generally is. In the interest of navigation we have to arrange to have icebreakers on hand.

Would it not be a good business proposition for the Government, instead of selling the icebreaker Lake Champlain for $61,000, to commission that vessel for doing this work under Government supervision, instead of letting the contract to a contractor to do the work on a basis of $40,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Lake Champlain is a very old icebreaker. She would not have been powerful enough to do the work, and then the cost of keeping her in commission all the year would be more expensive to the public than the Arrangement that we now have.

Amount required for two motor patrol vessels for buoy and lighthouse service in British Columbia, $15,000.
Does any part of this go to the yacht Narbethong?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid not.

I wish to congratulate the minister on the results obtained under this item. I notice that whereas last year the item called for $65,000, this year the item is only $15,000, a reduction of $50,000. Can the minister explain the reason for this reduction, because, if the requirements are the same, the reduction is enormous. If it is as it appears, a reduction in the services rendered, the minister deserves to be congratulated on this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think I am in for congratulations at all, although I appreciate the sentiments of my hon. friend. Last year the amount voted was $50,000; but it was not found sufficient, and, therefore, we are asking for $15,000 more to add on to that amount. I wish to explain to my hon. friend how that happened. The men who are building these two small boats are returned soldiers, and they put in the lowest tender. Then they came to Ottawa and told me that they could not finish the boats at the price at which they had tendered. They said that if we insisted on their doing so, they would

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

The beds in Richmond Bay, Prince Edward Island, where an epidemic broke out amongst the oysters some years ago, were examined. The disease is abating, but has not yet run its course. There are a few oysters left, and the only remedy is to let the disease run its full course, and then build the beds up again. Professor Robertson, of Toronto University, has been studying the situation and will continue to do so. The oyster situation is far from satisfactory, and it does not seem probable that it will improve until the divided jurisdiction between the provinces and the federal authorities is ended. At present the provinces have the leasing of areas for private culture, while the Dominion makes regulations ana supervises the public beds. The estimated cost of this service is $8,000.

I have a slight protest to make against the conduct of some officer or other; I do not know who is the guilty one. We have a large county with a coast line of about 100 miles, and last year the minister appointed an officer in the southern portion of the county. There was held an examination that had not been advertised, so far as people in the northern portion of the county were aware. That is to say the advertisement was not distributed in the northern portion of the county. I think my information is correct, that the examination was first held in the interior of the county some twenty miles away from the sea shore. I do not know how this was manipulated. It certainly was a process of manipulation because it so happened that when the examination was held two estimable young men from my own neighbourhood went to take it. They left the settlement in the night time and returned in the night time but unfortunately for them and mark well they were from the settlement where this examination was not 
advertised-the papers did not arrive in time. The examination was then changed to another section of the country-Port Hood. The examination was held there, ana I ask hon. gentlemen to mark this, the northern portion of the county where there are perhaps a thousand-yes fifteen hundred-families dependent on fishing, never knew anything about the examination. The result of course was that only a few people in the central portion of the county took that examination. Then, when the time came to appoint an officer in North Inverness, one of the men that had taken the examination was appointed, but he found it was necessary for him to move to the north end of the county, which was inconvenient for him to do and did not accept the post. The second appointee also refused to accept it. They then made a third appointment-a very estimable young man in whom I have every confidence. I am not reflecting on him, but I find fault with the course that was followed in reference to the examination. I consider it to be a serious cause for complaint that the northern portion of this county, which is almost exclusively a fishing community, should be deprived of the opportunity of taking this examination, resulting in the fact that the Government had to go some where else for an inspector. I want to make that protest although I do not know who is at fault.

I can tell my hon.
friend he is not presenting an isolated case.

That is pretty bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There seems to be a good deal in what my hon. friend says, but of course he understands I have nothing to do with the matter at all. These appointments are entirely in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. They are supposed to advertise them well, but if they have not done so all I can say is that I will bring my hon. friend's complaint to. their attention.	:

I think the minister is fair in that. I am not blaming the minister with what occurred, but of course he is responsible for the appointment of all the officials. If we have no one to speak to in regard to these appointments we might as well remain silent.
Who are the fishery overseers for the county of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We only have one, A. J. Evans of Chester.

After the argument made by the hon. member for Inverness, and the statement made by the hon. member for Frontenac that the Civil Service Commission made an appointment before the advertised date of the examination, it seems to me the House should take some action with regard to the work being done by that commission. I feel quite confident that the minister in his own business would not allow any kind of a commission to appoint his officials, and it seems to me that the same principle should apply in the matter of the appointment of Government officers. The minister has just made the statement that in the county of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, which is perhaps the most important fishing county in Canada, there is only one fishery officer in the service of the Government. Previously there were two fishery overseeers, one for the eastern end of the county and the other for the western end. The overseer for the western end resigned on June 8^ 1920, and that position has been vacant for almost ten months. Now I do not know who is to blame for that, but it seems to me that the Fisheries Department should not allow the Civil Service Commission to hold up this appointment for ten months. The district is a very important one, and there are a great many matters coming up from day to day which need the attention of a fishery overseer, and yet we have an	important fishing centre
like this	deprived	of his services.
Now note the effect of the failure to make this appointment. The sum of $160,000 is annually distributed in bounties to the fishermen on the Atlantic coast, and a great part of this bounty goes to fishing vessels and fishermen in Lunenburg county. Yet because of the fact that the Civil Service Commission have not appointed an overseer the department was put to the trouble and expense of sending out individual cheques to individual fishermen. In the past all cheques were sent to the fishery overseer and it was his duty to distribute them. In the present instance, as a result of the way the Civil Service Commission is handling the matter, the department was this year compelled to send out these cheques to individual fishermen with the result that in a great many cases-due to the fact that the department
did not know the addresses of these fishermen-complaints came in that the cheques were not delivered. I do not blame the department, but I think they should take sufficient interest in this matter to compel the Civil Service Commission to make the appointment. My attention was called to this matter several times, and I have had some correspondence not only with the minister and his officials, but with the officials of the Civil Service Commission. The latter have been humbugging with regard to the matter since last June, and there is absolutely no excuse for it. It is certainly the minister's duty to take some action instead of allowing this vacancy to remain for ten months. I am not particular who gets the appointment, it does not matter very much to me, but I do say that somebody should be appointed, and I would like to get an explanation from the minister if it is at all possible, why no appointment has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I find myself for once quite in accord with my hon. friend from Lunenburg. He is quite right in his statement that this position has been vacant since June last. My department frequently notified the Civil Service Commission about the vacancy, and we have systematically followed the matter up since but with no result.

It seems to me that some change should be made. If the minister at the head of this department, or the minister at the head of any department, is going to be treated like this by the Civil Service Commission it is time for the Government to take some action. I certainly think that if the minister had consulted the member for the county, or the defeated candidate, or somebody, the appointment would have been made long ago. An important position like this, whether it is in my own county or in any other county, should not be left vacant for ten months. While I do not want to suggest to the minister what he should do, nevertheless, if I were in his place, I would see that something was done. If no action was taktA I would go over the heads of the commission and make the appointment-I would never let a position like this remain open for such a long period. Let me tell the minister how they are humbugging him. As he says the vacancy occurred last June. The minister was good enough to write me, after I had communicated with him, and tell me he would immediately take the matter up with the Civil Service Commis-
(

sion. I found afterwards that the minister had done so, hut on going to the Civil Service Commission in November last I discovered the appointment had not been made. I asked them to show me the correspondence which they did, but they did not do anything from June until November. Four or five months elapsed before they did a single solitary thing-they had just left the matter open. Then in November, after I had written them several letters and protested against this delay, they advertised for applicants with the result that some time in November they received five applications. These applicants were men of anywhere from forty to fifty years of age, and they were compelled to go before an examiner like a lot of school boys and undergo a written examination on subjects which a high school student could not have answered. Fancy expecting men of forty or fifty years of age to sit down and take a written examination in reading and writing. They showed me some of the question papers afterwards, and the questions were such as I could not have answered or ten per cent of the members of this House either. This was the way they were going to select a fishery overseer. All that a man requires for the job is practical experience and a knowledge of the three R's. Yet this Civil Service Commission sitting in Ottawa, knowing nothing about the requirements for the position, asked these men of forty and fifty years of age to write on those examination papers. Nothing was done after the examination, and in February I took the matter up and asked why one of those men had not been appointed. Then I was told that none of them made a sufficient number of marks to warrant appointment. A second examination was held, and as the commission found the written examination was not satisfactory they decided on an oral test. They asked Professor Murray, of Dalhousie University, Mr. Ward Fisher, inspector of marine and fisheries, and a third man-to be selected by them-to sit as an examining board. This meant that the candidates had to travel from my county to Halifax, a distance of sixty miles, and take the oral examination. Professor Murray is a gentleman of culture and learning, but he knows absolutely nothing about the fisheries of Nova Scotia. It would have been far better had the Civil Service Commission chosen an examining board from the locality where the candidates live. That oral examination was held over two months ago, but the vacancy has not yet been filled.

It seems to me that it is time the minister took some strong action and either made the Civil Service Commission fill the vacancy or appointed some one himself.

Did the Civil Service
Commission give any reason for the delay from June to November? And was the appointment an important one?

The appointment was perhaps one of the most important in Nova Scotia. As I stated, a great many matters come up every day to be decided by this overseer. For instance, to show the hon. member for North Perth how important this appointment is, at the present time the fisheries overseer for the eastern end of the district, who has enough business of his own to attend to, has to come to the western end and do the work of this other man. There is no excuse for the delay.
Was any excuse given?

None whatever. The minister says he took it up with the Civil Service Commission. I took it up also, and I presume other people were active in the matter as well. The commission humbugged that appointment, and several others. It is about time that this House, who are the representatives of the people, took this matter out of the hands o'f the Civil Service Commission.

In regard to the appointment of new guardians, does the department decide that men over a certain age are ineligible; and is preference given to returned soldiers both as guardians and overseers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The preference is always given to returned soldiers both for guardians and overseers. We have not any age limit, but I do not think that any one would be appointed who was over sixty-five years, anyway.

The minister will be surprised if I tell him that in one particular case-and I am not going to name the parties involved-one of his overseers appointed a returned soldier, and a superior officer came along and said, "You cannot take that man. You must take this man here who is not a returned soldier." That was simply because of something or other in the manner of making application, the returned soldier not getting an opportunity because he did not see the advertisement.
I am sure the minister would be surprised to think that an officer of his department would under those circumstances dismiss a returned soldier and put in his place a man who was not a returned soldier.
That is frequently done.

It is not necessary that I should name any of these parties involved, but it will be a lesson for the minister's officers after this if they are told that they must carry out the desires of the minister. I think the minister made last year what I considered equivalent to a promise that men over thirty-five years of age would not be appointed as guardians. Perhaps I am wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that we endeavour to get overseers not over that age, but we have no age limit for ^ guardians.

As there is an appointment of an overseer to be made in my county, and as the minister tries to get men under
thirty-five years of age, I must express the Mew that very often a better man could be obtained over that age. The hon. member for Inverness spoke about a returned soldier being supplanted by a civilian, and I also gave an instance. I think the returned soldier should get the preference wherever he is able to fill the position; but it is quite possible in the case of a fisheries position, which calls for practical knowledge of the fisheries, that a returned soldier might not have the necessary qualifications, and consequently the department should be careful to see that they get properly qualified men. Of course, the returned soldier should get the preference wherever it f is possible, but I would not think the line should be tightly drawn if he has no qualification to fill an important position connected with the fisheries. In regard to age,
I do not think the minister should be held down to the age limit of thirty-five. I know many men fifty years of age and over who have been fishing for a number of years, have more practical experience and are better qualified than men of thirty-five.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The policy of the department has been to give preference always to the returned soldier, and we do not hold rigidly to the age limit of thirty-five; that is merely a guide.

speechtext: The difference is very easily explained. Heretofore the inspection of pickled fish has been voluntary; but at the last session of Parliament an Act was passed making the inspection of pickled fish compulsory*, and this is only now coming into effect.

I presume this amount is to pay officials under the Act which the minister has mentioned. I do not want to complain about the way in which the Act was passed, because I presume I might be accused of leaving Ottawa before Parliament. had prorogued. I notice however, in looking over the proceedings of the House that this amendment to the Fisheries Act was passed the very last day and practically the last hour of the session. In the Marine

and Fisheries Committee strong opposition was taken, not to the principle of the Bill or of the amendments, but to the amendments, because many members of the committee felt that it would be impossible for the present to carry out this inspection. The Opposition was taken by members from the Maritime Provinces-and I think most of the money for inspection of pickled fish will be spent and the inspection will be carried out in the Maritime Provinces- because they could not see clearly how the Act would work out. After the Bill was killed about three times in the committee, it was resurrected and brought down to the House in the dying moments of the session and passed. It seems to me, in view of all these circumstances, that the minister would be well advised if he did not appoint any officials or take 'any action until the matter was further discussed by the Marine and Fisheries Committee. I am not complaining very strongly, although I think it would have been far better if the Act had not been passed last session. In view of the fact that the Act is on the statute book and that other members of the committee and myself, who are interested in the fisheries of the Maritime Provinces, Cannot see how it is possible for the Government to work out a proper inspection of pickled fish, I would strongly urge, in the interest of the fishermen and the fisheries, that the minister take no further action until we have -further discussion and information. Personally, I would be delighted if it were possible in some way to have governmental inspection, because large sums of money are lost every year by people who purchase pickled herring or pickled mackerel which are not properly packed. Under the circumstances, I think it would be only a waste of money for the Government to appoint a number of inspectors; they would only be paying out a lot of money for nothing and causing a great deal of trouble to the fishermen of the Maritime Provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend, as well as some other hon. members, were opposed to this, but there has been a voluntary inspection of pickled fish for some years. My department circularized the packers in order to find out whether they were in favour of compulsory inspection, and the majority of the replies that we received indicated that there was a general demand that the inspection of pickled fish should be compulsory instead of voluntary. The additional cost of making the inspection compulsory instead of voluntary
is so small, being only $1,800 a year, and the advantages to be derived from compulsory inspection are so great, that I think the Government would be well advised in carrying this out. My hon. friend thought last year that inspectors were to go to the various packers and inspect the fish and the packages in which the fish was put up. That is not the way in which the inspection is to be carried out. The inspection is going to take place only at large assembly centres. Personally, I am a strong believer in Canada having standards for fish and compulsory inspection, in order that we may establish ourselves more firmly in foreign markets than we have so far been able to do.

My objection is not to the question of expense. If the thing was feasible, I would not oppose an expenditure of $50,000, because this is a very important matter. If the fish are not to be inspected at the fishermen's establishments, how does the minister expect to inspect the fish at centres? I do not understand what the minister means by " packers." The packers would be the fishermen. I presume, when he refers to " packers," he means the purchasers of these fish, not the fishermen. If the minister's idea is to have the inspection made after the fish are brought in from the fishermen to the purchasers, I do not see how it is possible to do any good, because it is impossible for, say, a dozen inspectors to inspect a thousand or two thousand barrels of herring when they come into the city of Halifax in one day. When a fish merchant buys these fish from the fisherman and pays for them, he cannot go back to the fisherman and claim a reduction if, after opening a barrel, he finds, for instance, there is an old oilcoat in the middle of the barrel, or that the barrel, instead of containing 200 pounds of fish, contains 150 pounds of fish and 50 pounds of salt. The merchant, therefore, has to bear the loss himself. All an inspector can do is to open one barrel out of fifty or a hundred, and that is no good. If the minister wants to have a standard for pickled fish, I agree with him if it is possible to bring that about. At the present time, if you send a carload of fish to Montreal or Toronto and the price drops, the first thing you know, you get a telegram from the buyer in Montreal or Toronto refusing to take delivery. Three months ago two carloads of herring which I sent to Toronto were rejected in that way, although the same kind of fish had been shipped to another man in Toronto who

did not utter a word of protest. The result was that we had to bring those two carloads of fish back, pay the freight from Nova Scotia to Toronto and from Toronto to Nova Scotia, because this man refused to take delivery. If the minister could devise some scheme whereby inspection could get over that difficulty and whereby the buyer would have to accept the governmental inspection as showing that the packages contained good fish, he would be doing something for the country and the fishermen. If an inspector is going to inspect only one barrel in fifty or a hundred, we shall have the same trouble as we have now, because merchants in Toronto or Montreal or the West Indies would say: "These fish are had and we will not take delivery of them." The Government is not going to have an inspector put the inspection brand on fish if he examines only one ox two barrels in a hundred, so that I cannot see how the thing is to be worked out. I am just as anxious as the minister that there should be proper inspection. The only man who can inspect fish properly is the man who buys the fish from the fisherman, because it is his duty to see that he gets value from the fisherman from whom he buys the fish. Unless the fish are to be inspected barrel by barrel in the fish house, I do not see how the minister' can possibly carry out the clauses of this Act.
Mr. BALLANTYNE My department intend to proceed very, very carefully. The regulations read as follows:
In carrying out an inspection of the fish in the containers, an inspecting officer shall open and examine one container in ten, when the lot consists of fifty or more containers, and one container in five, when the lot consists of less then fifty containers.
We have also sent the following information to all parties interested.
1.	Immediately after the passing of the amended Act a circular containing a clear and comprehensive summary of what the Act requires of coopers and packers, was distributed by the Department's Fishery Overseers to all firshermen, packers and dealers who handle pickled fish and to all coopers who make fish barrels.
2.	Before the end of the year complete copies of the Act and Regulations were distributed by the same means to the same people.
3.	The two permanent Inspectors have visited and are still visiting coopers' shops and sections of the Coast where pickled fish are packed for the purpose of giving instruction in and explaining the methods required by the new Act.
4.	During the month of March, public notices were posted up in all districts where pickled fish are packed or fish barrels made, reminding all concerned of the date on which the amended Act becomes operative and of the consequences of not complying with its requirements.

5.	Numerous inquiries in connection with the operation of the Act have been answered from Headquarters.
In view of the publicity we have already given to these regulations, and the fact that we intend to move carefully in this matter, I think my hon. friend will have no complaint to make when he sees how the Act works.

I am not making any complaint. I am trying to get some solution of this question. I would be very glad to see the department spend $50,000 on this work if we were going to get value from it, but the minister stated a moment ago that the inspectors will only examine one barrel out of ten, where the lots are fifty or over, and only one in five, where the lots are less than fifty. How can an inspector put the Government stamp on the balance of these fish when he has only examined one barrel out of ten, or one out of five? The one barrel he examines may be good and the other nine may be bad. At the present time, the fish merchants do the examining themselves. After years of experience they know pretty well who packs good fish and who packs poor fish, and when the fish are brought in by the fishermen and landed on the wharf, if the merchants have not sufficient inspectors to look after that lot of fifty barrels, we will say, immediately they do not pay for the whole lot then, but set a number of barrels aside and say, we will examine these later and pay you after we have gone over them if they have any doubt at all as to the way in which the fisherman packs his fish. I would be very glad to see the fish merchants relieved of the necessity of having to do this inspection themselves, and if the department would pay for a proper inspection, well and good, but there must be enough inspectors to inspect all the fish or the inspection is useless. Every ' barrel should be stamped with the Government stamp, as No. 1 or No. 2 fish, and then the man in Toronto or Montreal who buys the fish could not turn them back on the fish merchant and dispute the grade. Unless the minister adopts some scheme of that kind, whereby the merchants wil be protected, it seems to me it is useless for the Government to attempt the inspection.
I quite agree with the minister that it is wise to have some regulations with regard to packages. In the past the packages have been very poor. It is necessary that there should be better packages for putting up herring, mackerel and other fish. If the minister and his officials would see that

heavier packages, with iron hoops on both ends, were made by the coopers and used by the fishermen, they would be doing some good service to the fisheries of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will agree that the very fact that there is this compulsory inspection will make the fishermen more careful than they have been under the voluntary inspection system. As to examining every barrel, the Department of Agriculture for instance, when they are inspecting apples, do not inspect every barrel in a shipment, say, of 1,000 barrels, but only a certain number, and then if the inspectors are satisfied that the apples are all right, they put the Government stamp on all the barrels. Section 56 of the Act provides that:
Inspecting officers are not restricted to this scale, but, if need be, shall open as many containers as they may deem necessary to satisfy themselves that the fish are as represented by the marks on the containers.
We will have to trust to the inspectors using proper judgment, and also trust to a certain extent to the honesty of the fishermen.

What will happen if a
fisherman brings in fifty barrels of mackerel or herring and the inspector finds that they are bad? Is there any fine or penalty of any kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The fish would be marked "below grade", and the fisherman would be liable to a penalty. The maximum fine is $50.
Does the inspector impose the fine himself, or who takes action against the fisherman?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspector
would bring the offender before a local magistrate.

Item agreed to.
Salaries, construction and maintenance of fish breeding establishments, $365,000.

The other day I had the pleasure of sending to a minister a petition from the Board of Trade of Isle Verte, asking for the construction of a fish breeding establishment at the mouth of what was formerly known as the Salmon river, now known as the Green river. Is there any prospect of the department providing a fish breeding establishment there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The application of my hon. friend has not yet reached us, but
I suppose it will in due course, when we shall be very glad to give it our very best consideration.	[DOT]
Perhaps the minister will send one of his officers down there to make a report. 'That is all I will ask of him at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do as my hon. friend suggests.

This is a very large item, $365,000. How much of this will be spent in the province of Ontario for fish breeding purposes? Does the Government maintain this service in Ontario? Did they in the past? If 'so, and the service has been discontinued, what is the reason? I get a great many letters from time to time from gentlemen who desire to get young fish or fry for stocking Ontario streams. In the past they used to get both bass and speckled trout from the Dominion Government, but I understand they are unable to get them now. If that is the case, I should like to know the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have eight
hatcheries in Ontario, for commercial species only.
What is covered by the term "commercial species", and where are these hatcheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The term "commercial species" includes whitefish, salmon, trout, herring and pickerel from the Great Lakes.
Where,are these hatcheries located?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At Sarnia, Collingwood, Port Arthur, Southampton, Thur-low, Kenora, Kingsville and Wiarton.
A fish-breeding establishment was built on Buctouche beach some years ago and was closed down about two years since. Why was this done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member has reference to lobster hatcheries. The department closed up all hatcheries in the Maritime Provinces about two years ago because they were of no benefit in any way.
Is there any fish-breeding establishment in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At Qu'Appelle.

What kind of fish is
bred there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Whitefish.
Any other varieties?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not that we know of.

I understand that these
fish are distributed to the lakes throughout the province of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We do distribute
these small fish throughout the province as far as we can.

Under what system is
this distribution made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: After consultation with the local fishery officer, we supply-the small fry to the waters we consider best adapted to their culture.
How is that determined? Is an analysis made of the waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The local fishery officer out there is perfectly familiar with the waters, and what with his advice and the knowledge of the officers of my department, we are able to come to a decision.

What fish-breeding
establishments are there in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are establishments at Bedford, Margaree, Windsor, Middleton, and Lindloff, near St. Peters.
Has the minister any information as to whether there is any improvement in salmon fishing along the coast since the hatchery at Margaree was built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Conditions have changed in Margaree, and the fish coming to that particular river have been far from satisfactory within the last two years.

That is not really the information I am after. The Margaree has been a very good salmon fishing river in years past, and when I was a boy its waters teemed with salmon. Of recent years, however, this particular industry has gone down considerably. I am not at all attributing this to the fact that therd is a hatchery on the river, but it has often occurred to me that it would be a good idea for the minister, through his officers, to study conditions there. It is too bad that a large amount of money should be expended keeping a hatchery going there if the salmon are becoming scarcer every year. The minister says that salmon are scarce in the Margaree river. I think what he has in mind is the fact that the hatchery has not all the salmon it would 
like to get for spawning purposes. That is not due entirely to any scarcity of salmon in the river; it is due to other conditions. I fear that perhaps the trap has not been set early enough, and I suspect that it has not been operated as correctly as it should be. That would explain the situation. There is an abundance of salmon there to fill all the hatcheries in Canada in the fall of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter has already been referred to the Biological Board, with instructions to them to make a thorough investigation and to report accordingly. If, as the hon. member says, there are plenty of salmon, there must be something wrong.

We have two kinds of salmon, spring salmon during June, July and August, which is the important variety in Margaree, and fall salmon. The spring fishing has gone down within the last four or five years, although it was a successful industry in the past.

Although I am not much of a fisherman myself, I know that in earlier years Margaree was considered the finest fishing river in Nova Scotia, and even to-day it is the second best river in the province. There is a successful industry in the Medway and in the Liverpool river, but in the latter they suffer from a multiplicity of dams, although the minister is trying to remedy that difficulty. I can say that the salmon fisheries in these three rivers, two of which are in my constituency, have been a source of much profit to fishermen, and they are a branch of our public affairs that well deserves all the consideration the minister can give them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The information
given by the member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm), regarding spring salmon is correct, and is in accordance with our own experience; but we are referring the whole matter to the Biological Board and hope to be able to devise some means of improving conditions.
In reference to the question asked by the member for Battle-ford (Mr. Wright), are other varieties besides whitefish, bred in the province of Saskatchewan? If not, why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hatchery has been breeding only whitefish. As the hon. member comes from that district, perhaps he has some suggestions to offer.
I did not quite catch the minister's remark.

I find that the total for this item last year-that is to say the year 1920-21-was $365,000 and according to the Auditor General's Report the expenditures for that year amounted to $305,476 a difference of $59,524, and that the Estimate for 1921-22 is for the same amount $365,000, or practically twenty per cent more than what was required for last year. This is a large difference, and I cannot see the reason for asking a vote for so much more than experience has shown to be required. I would like to know what explanation the minister has to give.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is not very much difference between the vote asked for and the actual expenditure for last year. The figures I have are only up to February 28, and they show an amount of $332,085 as having been expended. To this we would have to add the expenditure for the month of March which would only make a difference of possibly $15,000 between~the vote we are asking and the actual expenditure.

That is quite satisfactory. I find on page R-76 of the Auditor General's Report for 1919-20 some items as to which I would like an explanation. Would it be in order for me to put these questions, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, if they have reference to this matter.

I find in the first place at the page of the Auditor General's Report already given, under the heading of advertising, an amount of $288.25. Further down the page appears an item of $952.32 for printing and stationery, and the two items total $1,240.57. I would like to know the reason of so much expenditure on advertising?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: :Would my hon. friend tell me what appropriation these amounts have been charged to?

To "Fish Breeding;
General Account."	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the information regarding the past year's transactions before me but it may have been for calling for tenders for the erection of hatcheries.

I would consider this a very large expenditure for an item of that
kind but I suppose we will have to let it go with the explanation given by the minister. I find another item on the same page, charged to the same account:
Fooks, Harry, Agassiz, B.C.; funeral expenses of the late Lawrence Ogilvie, $297.65.
What relation has this to fish breeding?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One of our employees named Mr. Ogilvie was drowned while on official duty and that was the compassionate allowance paid to his heirs. If there is any other information my hon. friend wants I would be very glad to look up last year's figures and send it to him.

There are two other items I would like to make inquiry about:
Burton, L. J.; Expenses locating site for salmon hatchery in East Nova Scotia, $401.52; sundry expense, $13.25, $414.77.
That seems a large amount to pay for a trifling bit of work of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It costs a good deal for travelling and hotel expenses, and that is what that amount is for.

There is another item under the same heading of "Fish Breeding" :
Gowan, G. H., K.C., Vancouver, legal expenses in connection with fisheries inquiry before Mr. Justice Eberts, $2,289.
MacEay, P. J.; Vancouver; transcribing proceedings held before Mr. Justice Eberts, $1,176.90.
What was the nature of this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Justice Eberts was instructed to look into matters in district No. 3, British Columbia. The first amount my hon. friend mentioned was for legal expenses paid to Mr. Cowan.
What was the object of the investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Charges of irregularities made against certain fishery officers out there which justified my department in asking Justice Eberts to hold an investigation. He did so but his report has not yet been submitted to us.
The investigation was held in the year 1919-20, and the judge has not yet reported whether the charges were sustained or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. My hon.
friend may be interested in learning that no later than to-day I was endeavouring to stir the matter up. It is now in the hands of our own Justice De-



partment and the Minister of Justice is doing everything he can to have the report forwarded. There has been a long delay.

A moment or two
ago I asked the minister if his department had introduced the breeding of any other varieties of fish than white fish in the province of Saskatchewan. I did not hear the minister's reply but he asked me for some suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister be
good enough to answer my question as to whether the department has ever attempted anything in the direction of breeding other varieties of fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My answer is
"No". We have never attempted the breeding of other fish than white fish.

Reports have been
made to me that other varieties of fish would do pretty well in the inland waters of Saskatchewan, and it has been .suggested that the people out there be supplied with fry of dore, pickerel, and bass.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not intend to make any definite promise, but it is the intention of my department to move in the direction that my hon. friend has suggested almost immediately.

The amount asked for this particular service is a very large one- $365,000, and I think that before the item passes some consideration should be given to it. I have taken some interest in the matter of fish culture and I have accumulated a good deal of information that I would like to place before the committee. However, on account of the fact that my throat is in bad condition and I am not able to articulate very plainly, and also in view of the fact that the attendance of members is very small, I would like the minister to be good enough to allow this item to stand and permit the discussion on it to take place later. In the meantime, in order to show the minister how seriously I regard this matter, I may tell him that I believe the most of this money is absolutely wasted. I should be most happy to lay my views before the committee to-night but unfortunately I am not able to do so.

I hope the minister
will be able to comply with the request of the hon. gentleman. The hon. member represents one of the greatest fishing districts in the Dominion. He gives a great deal of attention to this subject, he has carefully studied it, and has information which,

I am sure, the minister will be glad to receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am very sorry
my hon. friend's throat is in the condition it apparently is, and on account of that I will be glad to pass the item over.
Item stands.
To provide for scientific investigation into practical economic problems connected with the fisheries, $15,000.

Mr. Chairman, I think under that item I would be in order if I called the attention of the minister to the question-the very vexed question as it has been in times past-of the lobster season. I know he has given it a great deal of study and has made very earnest efforts to meet the wishes of the various sections of the country. Unfortunately regulations which will suit in some districts do not suit in others. I think he may very fairly claim that in the main his regulations have given satisfaction over a very considerable district. There is, however, a section of the province which feels that it ought to have the privilege of fishing in the early winter season. The lobster season in the western section of Nova Scotia begins the first of March. The winter season is so expensive in eastern Nova Scotia that no fishing in the winter is desired, no matter-what season you allow them there, because of the cost of equipment and the danger from storms. But in my counties of Shelburne and Queen's and notably Shelburne, the people can carry on a very considerable fishing season in the months of No.vember and December, when lobsters are very much in demand in the American market. The geographical position of the county is such that the fishermen have easy access to the American market, and during the past winter it has been felt to be quite a hardship that during several months when there is absolute idleness in the fishing districts, they should be deprived of lobster fishing. That is notably so in Shelburne county and in the western part of Halifax county. In some sections of the western part of Halifax county the fishermen are not at any time too prosperous, and during the past winter I think representations were made to the minister that'the absence of winter fishing worked a very great hardship to them. Some other kinds of the fishing business had not prospered and the fishermen were exceedingly anxious to be allowed to conduct winter fishing in that section.
I have also a stronger reason to urge the minister to reconsider the question in re-

spect to the counties of Shelburne and Queen's. It is said very often: "What is the use of having this winter season? The cost of equipment and damage to the gear is such that very little fishing would be done." Well, those who do not want winter fishing need not take it; it is not compulsory. But there is a very considerable section in the county of Shelburne which would highly appreciate this winter fishing, and men engaged in the business are firmly persuaded that no injury would result to any other section of the province. I do not say this in a complaining spirit, for I know the difficulties of the matter, the conflict between the different sections, and I know the effort the minister made by calling a convention at Halifax in order to get the best advice available. He carried out the conclusions which that convention reached. That convention, however, was very largely a packers' convention; unfortunately the fishermen were not very generally represented. At all events, I would ask the minister, notwithstanding his refusal in the past to allow any winter fishing-I am not complaining of that refusal-whether he cannot consider hereafter permitting winter fishing to such portions of the province as are willing to avail themselves of it. The men engaged in lobster fishing do very well in a short time, and therefore perhaps do not give as much attention as they should to other branches, but it is a fact that during the winter season a very large number of our fishermen are idle, and that at a time when they should be earning a very considerable amount of money in lobster fishing without any great disadvantage to any other part of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The question of
winter lobster fishing that my hon. friend has just brought to my attention again is well worth further consideration by me and the technical officers of the department. I will be very glad to go very carefully into it again and let my hon. friend know if it is not possible to meet his wishes.

Item agreed to.
International Commission, Fraser River, $10,000. . [DOT]
What is this International Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An International
Commission was appointed in 1918 to visit British Columbia and look into the salmon conditions there. An agreement was drawn up and is now before the American Senate. It did receive the approval of President
139i
Wilson, but it will not come into effect until it is approved by the American Senate. It will also have to be approved by this House. The matter is just in statu quo. We are asking for the vote in the hope that the American Senate will approve of the agreement, and then the matter will be brought before this House.
How are the expenses of this Commission divided between the two nations interested, Canada and the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The treaty provides for the appointment of an International Commission composed of four members, two from each country, to conduct investigations into the life history of the. salmon, hatchery methods, suitable ground conditions, and other related maters, and to recommend to their respective governments any modifications or additions to or substitutions for the appended regulations which may be found desirable.
It is according to a treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
, Item agreed to.
Marine Biological Board of Canada, $42,000.

This seems to be quite a large item and I do not understand just exactly what it is for. I hold in my hand the Auditor General's Report, and at page R-76 I find a statement of expenditure at St. Andrew's, N.B., amounting to $16,894.59. I think the head of the institution is Dr. A. G. Huntsman. What work is being done there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The work of the
Biological Board is purely scientific-looking into fish life and matters pertaining thereto. The expenditure for last year amounted to $26,000. We are asking for $16,000 more because the accommodation at the St. Andrew's biological station will have to be increased. The gentlemen composing this Board are professors of our leading universities, and they give their services gratuitously, the Bilogical Board paying their travelling expenses when they are called to meet at Ottawa.
Do they prepare and distribute reports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Where can we get those reports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not one at hand, but I will be glad to mail a copy to my hon. friend.

I would like to see what work is being done at the St. Andrew's station. The minister should be able to advise the committee if this work is of importance and is of any advantage to the fishing industry.
I find on page R-77 of the Auditor General's Report a reference to " brass messengers." Would the minister tell me what these are?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know just what they are-probably something used in the laboratory.

Item agreed to.
Civil government-Marine and Fisheries- salaries, $360,810 ; contingencies, $68,870.

I find in the details of this item provision for one purchasing agent, $3,900; one assistant purchasing agent, $2,800; one junior purchasing agent, $2,100; one senior supplies clerk, $2,600; one supplies clerk, $1,600; one at $1,$250; one at $1,200; total, $15,450. What are the duties of these purchasing agents? I have been informed by ministers of other departments that similar purchasing agents in their departments merely make out the requisitions and pass them on to the Purchasing Commission and there their duties end. Is that the case with these officers of my hon. friend's department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The purchasing
agent of the Department of Marine attends to all the details which would be looked after by any purchasing agent. He deals with the requisition, makes sure that the quantity is not too much and that the articles in question are really needed; calls for public tenders and gets everything in shape for the submission to the deputy minister and also to myself as minister. After that is done, the matter is passed to the Purchasing Commission for final decision.

Then of what value is the Purchasing Commission in a transaction of that kind? What service do they render for the $80,000 odd which is being appropriated for their expenses? Could this work not he performed by the organization already in operation in my hon. friend's department, without the services of that Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My opinion, of course, would be the same as that expressed on behalf of the Government by my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). There are statutes governing the powers of a minister, but I do not think it was ever claimed that the Purchasing 
Commission had statutory authority. They were given certain powers, however, by Order in Council; their business is to collaborate all the statistics and work in the closest harmony with all the purchasing clerks connected with the various departments. Their work is of a supervisory character, the details being very largely attended to by the department.

I understand from the minister that these purchasing operations are supervised by the deputy minister and that in some cases the minister himself has to pass upon them. Why, then, the necessity of the Purchasing Commission? The minister has in his department a number of officials designated as senior, junior and assistant purchasing clerks, supplies clerks, and so on, costing the country some $15,000 a year. These officials appear to he performing the necessary duties in connection with purchases. The purchasing agent himself receives a salary of $3,900 a year, with bonus in addition. If he is a real purchasing agent he is not sufficiently paid; if he is merely a requisition clerk he is getting too much. But it would seem that the work would be just as well done by the organization under the supervision of the deputy minister, and in some cases of the minister himself; and the only conclusion I can come to is that the Purchasing Commission is an unnecessary expense and that the Government should dispense with it at once.

It appears from what the minister says that after tfie requisitions are prepared by this official and submitted to the deputy minister and then to the minister they are passed along to the Purchasing Commission. Is it to be inferred from this that the Purchasing Commission may override the decision of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Minister of Marine and of the Naval Service is governed by statute; the Purchasing Commission would have no authority to over-ride his decision. But it was the experience that the War Purchasing Commission effected large savings and the Government thought it wise to continue, not the same personnel, but a purchasing commission as a supervisory body. They have more freedom than other departments that are not working under statutes like the Minister of Marine.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
